newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil unveils plan to keep grip on deficit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil unveils plan to keep grip on deficit.

text.p: The Brazilian government unveiled on Friday an extensive package of measures to curb federal spending, eliminate jobs and boost tax revenues in a bid to improve fiscal accounts while major reforms sit in Congress.

The package, which will also bolster the social security system and oblige state-owned companies to sell off non-operational assets, should give the government a net gain of 6.5 billion reais in 1997, Finance Minister Pedro Malan said.
"We believe this fiscal adjustment gives continuity to our efforts to approve constitutional reform in Congress, which we will not abandon," Malan told reporters.
The new measures, included in a battery of decrees, resolutions and acts, meant Brazil's operational deficit stood a chance of being under 2.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1997, he said.
Malan said he expected the deficit to be equivalent to about 3.5 percent of GDP in 1996, down from five percent in 1995.
The following were the main points of the package:
-- the elimination of more than 100,000 civil service posts in the federal government, of which about 73,000 are currently occupied, plus the axing of 94,000 posts in state-owned firms;;
-- the sale or liquidation of non-operational assets of state-owned companies;
-- a ceiling on the payrolls of state-owned companies to bring about an 11 percent saving in 1997 compared with 1996;
-- the auditing of state-owned companies with a view to their inclusion in the National Privatization program;
-- approval of a new law to speed up the approval of splitting subsidiaries from holdings prior to privatization, which would hasten power and telecommunications selloffs;
-- the hiring of 2,000 new tax officials to boost revenues;
-- a crackdown on tax debtors and the sale of confiscated goods to raise a total of about two billion reais;
-- an end to "unjustifiable privileges" of civil servants' including promotions for workers about to retire, generous holidays, overtime pay and the accumulation of pensions;
-- simplification of rules for contributors to the national social security system to increase revenues.

A document produced the ministers of finance, planning, social security and administration said the federal government's payroll spending rocketed to 42.3 billion reais in 1995 from 20.7 billion reais in 1992.
The increase was mostly due to the success of government's economic stabilization plan which denied it the traditionally corrosive effect of inflation on the real value of outlays.
The document also said the social security system was heading for a 1.5 billion-reais deficit in 1996, up from 400 million reais in 1995.
